newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Bonn pelted with criticism over unemployment.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bonn pelted with criticism over unemployment.

text.p: Growing concern at Germany's relentlessly high jobless levels prompted a barrage of criticism on Sunday with one union leader calling on Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government to admit defeat and step down.

Unions, politicians and economists clashed over how to combat rising unemployment and were at odds over whether sluggish economic growth, the absence of structural reform, or the length of the working week was to blame.

"It is high time for this government to step down," Klaus Zwickel, chairman of the IG Metall union told a weekend meeting in Hannover. Bonn had failed to fullfil its promises, and the public was fed up with trusting in higher corporate turnover and "exploding" profits to reduce unemployment, he said.
Zwickel, the head of Germany's largest trade union, in June called for the average working week to be cut to 32 hours.

Retaliating against what he termed Zwickel's "one-sided, party political propaganda", Peter Hintze, general secretary of Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), said the union leader's policy of reducing working hours had led only to rising labour costs and the destruction of jobs.
"We need an investment-friendly climate which will create new jobs," Hintze said. "Greater flexibility and a reduction in labour costs are needed for that."
He said the IG Metall chief should abstain from such "crass polemics" and concentrate instead on cooperation to secure Germany's position.
Latest figures show that 4.26 million people are out of work in Germany, 11.1 percent of the workforce.
Juergen Ruettgers, also a CDU minister, said eduction and training were the way foreward, urging his party to take the issue of apprenticeships seriously.

But Horst Siebert, a leading German economist and a member of the government's "five wise men" economic advisory council, said the country must undergo far-reaching reform of the social welfare system to ease unemployment levels.

Lashing out at the stability and jobs pact agreed by Eureopan leaders in Amsterdam, Siebert said such agreements were of litle use in the fight against joblessness, since its causes were different in every country.

Germany's labour markets were suffering above all under the burden of high wage levels and structual problems, and relying on an expected pick-up in growth rates was not enough. "Growth alone cannot eliminate Germany's jobs crisis," he told the Welt am Sonntag newspaper.
Criticism of the EU Amsterdam deal was also levelled by Heide Simonis, state premier for Schleswig Holstein and a member the opposition Social Democats (SPD).
"(The pact) is nothing but empty phrases. It was formulated very vaguely so that no-one would lose face," he told the weekly Spiegel magazine Germany.
Simonis said Germany should introduce job-sharing initiatives, cut working hours and wages accordingly, and consider a reduction in the minimum starting wage for the long-term unemployed.

In an interview with Sunday's Frankfurter Allegemeine newspaper, Klaus Freidrich, cheif economist of Dresdner Bank AG, said fascination in media and political circles with the impending euro single currency was drawing attention away from the "far greater problem" issue of conquering unemployment.

While he said the euro, due to come into being with the third stage of European economic and monetary union (EMU) in January 1999, would not in itself improve the employment situation, he said a future without a single currency offered no better perspective.
